articles.title: Next StarCraft Game Announced at BlizzCon as an Open-World Shooter, but It’s Not Due Out Until 2030
articles.summary: It’s been over 15 years since Blizzard’s beloved real-time strategy game, StarCraft 2, came out. Now, a new game in the series has been announced — but it’s still years away.
articles.body:
It’s been over 15 years since Blizzard’s beloved real-time strategy game, StarCraft 2 , came out. Now, a new game in the series has been announced — but it’s still years away.

Revealed at BlizzCon 2026, the simply named StarCraft is the next title in the sci-fi franchise, and it’s going to look markedly different from its predecessors.

In fact, it’s a completely different genre. StarCraft is an open-world shooter, and it’s due out in 2030. While this distant launch window makes it hard to get too excited about StarCraft just yet, Blizzard has a history of announcing games far before they're ready for the public to play. In fact, it’s something the company behind Warcraft, Diablo, and Overwatch is notorious for doing, historically touting the mantra: “It’ll be ready when it’s ready.”

The announcement of a new StarCraft game was expected at BlizzCon, after the official StarCraft website became rife with visual ‘glitches,’ and issued a ‘warning’ telling users their device has been “compromised.” Fans took this to mean that a big update for the franchise was on the horizon, and they were right.

Indeed, rumors of a StarCraft shooter had been circling for years. In 2024, Bloomberg reporter Jason Schreier told IGN’s Podcast Unlocked about Blizzard’s third attempt at developing a StarCraft shooter with former Far Cry executive producer Dan Hay, who joined Blizzard in 2022, leading the charge. Then, later in 2024, a job posting was listed for an ‘upcoming open-world shooter’ that fans were certain was tied to this StarCraft game.

Blizzard has had a tough time developing StarCraft shooters over the years. StarCraft Ghost , announced in 2002, was going to be a tactical-action console game in which you played as a deadly Ghost operative in the employ of the Dominion, but it was canceled in 2006 after a series of delays.

A second attempt to make a StarCraft shooter, codenamed Ares, was canceled in 2019 so Blizzard could focus on Diablo 4 and Overwatch 2 . Ares was reportedly “like Battlefield in the StarCraft universe,” but, like Ghost, fell by the wayside.

Now, it’s a case of third time lucky for Blizzard with this new StarCraft shooter in development. Check out everything announced at BlizzCon 2026 for all the news from across Blizzard.

articles.title: X-Men Star Inde Navarrette Teases Her Plan to Nail Rogue’s Southern Accent
articles.summary: Obsession breakout Inde Navarrette already has a plan to make sure she nails Rogue's iconic Southern accent in the new X-Men movie.
articles.body:
Obsession breakout Inde Navarrette already has a plan to make sure she nails Rogue's iconic Southern accent in the new X-Men movie .

Navarrette will jump from horror to the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU) when she appears in X-Men in 2028. As revealed last month, it's due out May 5, 2028, but even more than Rogue's power-stealing abilities and fierce attitude, fans have been dying to know if Navarrette will bring any spice to Rogue's voice.

The character is known for her southern draw, especially thanks to the delivery made popular by original X-Men animated series voice actress Lenore Zann . Navarrette may not have the natural accent audiences would expect from Rogue, but she told Entertainment Tonight that the mutant team member's voice is very much already on her mind.

"I've never told this publicly – I completely forgot – but I have a divorced family. I grew up in Texas for a good majority of my life," Navarrette said when asked how she'll build Rogue's voice. "So, honestly, those Southern women are really my favorite."

Navarrette then noted her specific connection to Corpus Christi, a coastal town located toward the south end of Texas. For the Obsession actress-turned-Marvel superhero, it's the "old Southern women" that she "really, really loves." But her appreciation for the South doesn't stop there.

"But, specifically, Mississippi – Rogue is from Mississippi," she continued. "So, I really just want to go there. I wanna really do her justice."

Navarrette is just one piece of a grander MCU puzzle. Also confirmed for the big MCU X-Men reboot movie are Adam Driver as Mister Sinister, Maya Boyd as Storm, Christopher Abbott as Professor X, Sadie Sink as Jean Grey, Kit Connor as Cyclops, and Samara Weaving as Emma Frost. Gen V and Scream 7 star Asa Germann was also recently picked to play the winged mutant, Angel .

So many other pieces need to come together before X-Men arrives, but director Jake Schreier has teased a team-up movie worth waiting for. In August, he talked about some of the comic books he's looking to for inspiration , promising to give MCU fans a movie that is a "new spin" on what they've seen with past live-action X-Men films. Meanwhile, Navarrette is reportedly so excited to do the movie that she passed up a part in Heat 2 .

articles.title: Diablo 5 Forging the Next Era Panel: Everything Announced
articles.summary: Blizzard has revealed three classes for Diablo 5, a first look at its UI, and shown off even more as part of its Forging the Next Era panel at BlizzCon 2026.
articles.body:
Blizzard has revealed three classes for Diablo 5, a first look at its UI, and shown off even more as part of its Forging the Next Era panel at BlizzCon 2026 .

The next Diablo game might be years away from its spring 2029 launch, but that didn't stop some members of the development team from confirming the first details. Highlights from the 45-minute panel include confirmation that the Demon Hunter and Monk are two returning classes, but a new class is coming too: the Plague Knight.

Concept art, gameplay details, and more were all revealed as part of the big panel presentation. Blizzard also talked about why it decided to make the announcement now, almost three years before launch. We gathered all of the highlights for newcomers and die-hard fans to comb through right here. You can see everything announced at the Diablo 5 BlizzCon panel below.

Multiple members from the Diablo team have taken the stage at BlizzCon 2026. After the surprise reveal for Diablo 5, it's clear the developers have a lot to talk about. Shely said the plan is for the panel to cover the story, world, gameplay, and even some information about itemization.

"We're a long way from the campfire, from its comfort and hope. These are the fires of Diablo. Sanctuary has been destroyed, and Diablo has won," Shely said.

Producer Matt Zitterman said, when deciding how to approach more Diablo, Blizzard first had to decide whether to do more DLC or another mainline entry. When looking at Diablo 4 and an opportunity to bring back the true Diablo, a proper sequel with Diablo 5 is the only thing that really made sense.

"Once we decided that this game was going to bring Diablo back, we knew we had to do it right," narrative director Jennifer Brandes Hpler said. "He couldn't just be a final boss. He needs to be a boss that's shaping this game from its opening moments. That's how we decided that, this time, you're not scrambling to shape Sanctuary before Diablo tries to take it over."

Shely added that Diablo "has a lot more to say" in this game. Don't expect Diablo to have some tragic backstory in Diablo 5, though.

"Pretty quickly we kept arriving at the same conclusion: Diablo is Diablo. He is the Lord of Terror," senior producer Tiffany Wat said. "He's not redeemable. He's not misunderstood. That gave us a lot of clarity, so the question now becomes not 'Is he right?' but 'What happens now that he's won?'"

Shely teased that returning to Westmarch will see players confronting a place that has become an "outpost of Hell." That means very few humans have not bowed to the Lord of Terror or become cultists, with some humans even turning to become Dread Commanders, which harness the power of the Dukes of Hell.

Blizzard also confirmed terrain will change when players return to certain areas. Procedural worlds are also coming back with Diablo 5.

"That idea of not knowing what's around the corner creates a lot of tension," Wat said. "So, in Diablo 5, we're bringing back the procedural world, both in the dungeons and the overworld. So, if you go back to a region that you've been before, all that information knew yesterday - that path that I found, that landmark that I was moving toward, how to fight those Elite monsters - none of that is information is going to help me today."

Diablo fans know Treasure Goblins to be "loot pinatas," but in Diablo 5, one character will change that. Wat teased Zarg, a new character and a Treasure Goblin that players will grow to know. His name's not final and neither are his character details, but he's yet another sign that Blizzard is shaking things up for its next big installment.

Shely teased some of the classes coming to Diablo 5. The Demon Hunter and Monk are two returning classes coming to the game. New classes are coming, too, including the heavily armored Plague Knight, which will see players spreading disease and then consuming it for power. That's all he was willing to tease today, but he did say that Diablo 5 will launch with more classes than any other entry than ever before.

"I don't just mean just more classes than any Diablo game at ship," he elaborated. "I mean more classes total. The thing about Diablo classes is they're approachable - you can jump in and immediately have an exciting time playing them - but there's also deep ARPG mastery there and a multitude of builds to explore."

Diablo 5 is still very early in development, so how it handles itemization is still being put together. However, the team was willing to share a sneak peek at concept art for what things look like in this stage of work. Gear-based sets are coming back, with Shely also confirmed that there will be multi-slot items.

"I like to think of itemization kind of like a city," Shely said. "Think about New York City; It's an enormous metropolis, you can immediately go to Time Square and immediately find something cool. That's kind of how I think about our set up. Once you really start to dig in and master it, you learn where's the best deli, where's the best pizza, and you really get into that crunchy opportunity to define your own builds. That's what we want to do in D5."

This is more from Diablo 5 many likely expected to see, but Blizzard doesn't want fans to be overwhelmed by the image they see here. Shely teased that they've got some "really great solutions for any controller players who might be worried about manipulating those items."

All of the words shared by the Diablo team during the Forging the Next Era BlizzCon 2026 panel are all fine and good, but some fans may be worried that, with years to go until launch, there's no telling what the final product will look like. Zitterman promised that Diablo 5 is a game they hope to build alongside the community, which is why we're learning about it years before its planned launch.

"I think for us it's super important that Diablo 5 feels unmistakably Diablo, in particular for our longtime players," Zitterman said. "That starts with what I talked about at the beginning: Understanding who are Diablo players at their core? What do they want, what do they need, out of a Diablo game?"

He continued: "When you're building a game, you need other people to look at your work and give you that critical feedback. We want to get that feedback now. We want to get that feedback as early as possible. It's why we're announcing today. It's why we're excited to bring the community into the process of making the game along the way toward our launch date."

Zitterman signed off the news portion of the panel by telling players that they won't have to wait long for updates. The plan is for the team to share "regular updates about how development is going" starting in 2027.

"We talked about how D5 will let you define your identity, discover builds, chase memorable loot, right?" Shely added. "More than that, our job is to build the game players want - that you want. Not what we think you should want. We want to build the best Diablo game, and that means listening to you; listening to your feedback, and allowing it to shape the game."

Image courtesy of Blizzard Entertainment.

articles.title: StarCraft returns in 2030 as an open-world shooter
articles.summary: 10 years after the last StarCraft II expansion pack the series is finally being brought back to life.
articles.body: Blizzard originally tried to bring the StarCraft universe to the world of 3D shooters way back in 2002 with StarCraft: Ghost. It sat in development hell for years until Blizzard president Mike Morhaime confirmed that it had been canceled in 2014. Now Blizzard is giving it another go with the simply titled StarCraft. Dan Hay, a VP at Blizzard, took the stage at BlizzCon today to reveal that after more than a decade of lying dormant, StarCraft would be returning in 2030. But, rather than another top-down real-time strategy installment, the new title would be an open-world shooter. He then showed off a cinematic trailer for the title that focused on the human United Earth Directorate faction as they prepare to face off against the Zerg. The Protoss are limited to passing mention. What’s obvious from the trailer is that the new take on the StarCraft franchise won’t be pulling many punches. After a rousing call to militarism, the propaganda-fueled human is faced with the brutal realities of battle, and the character we’ve been following for the last 3 minutes is revealed to be disposable fuel for the meat grinder of war. [Media: While fans are definitely excited that Blizzard is defrosting the long-dormant series, I’m sure plenty are still holding their breath, hoping for a proper RTS follow-up to 2010’s StarCraft II.

articles.title: Warcraft 3 Reforged: Forsaken Kingdom Review So Far
articles.summary: A surprise single-player campaign that maintains the feel of classic Warcraft 3 while mixing in some new ideas.
articles.body:
If you're a bit stunned to hear that there's a new single-player story campaign for Warcraft 3 in 2026 – 23 years after its last expansion, The Frozen Throne – then you can imagine how I felt when Forsaken Kingdom fell into my hands ahead of its surprise announcement and immediate release today. It's honestly great to be back, considering Blizzard hasn't given single-player RTS fans anything new to chew on at all since 2016's Starcraft II: Nova Covert Ops. This expansion maintains the feel of classic Warcraft 3 while mixing in some new ideas, and that's something I might never run out of appetite for.

At the time of writing, I've only had the chance to play through maybe a quarter of the new story: the four-mission Last Days of Lordaeron prologue, which is quite juicy and ambitious on its own, as well as the first three or so hours of what Blizzard says is roughly 30 total in Forsaken Kingdom. The latter really leans into being an RPG so far, like a more ambitious version of Rexxar's Founding of Durotar bonus campaign in The Frozen Throne.

The Last Days of Lordaeron picks up on the day Arthas returned from Northrend to kill his father, perhaps one of the most pivotal moments in all of Warcraft lore, and follows the new hero, guard lieutenant Garek Bandarion, as he fights his way through a besieged Andorhal and a devastated Strathholme in a doomed attempt to save his homeland from the Scourge. This prologue culminates with a confrontation against none other than Baron Rivendare, and contains numerous clever little references to both Warcraft 3 and World of Warcraft.

I enjoyed the design of these missions for the most part. The Siege of Andorhal, especially, puts a little bit of a MOBA-inspired twist on the typical Warcraft 3 routine by having you capture towers that spawn waves of AI-controlled friendly soldiers at regular intervals to help you push across the map. Another segment of the same mission required me to hold specific objectives to be able to recruit certain kinds of units, rather than simply needing their associated structure in my base.

Stratholme, post-purge at this point, is built like a winding dungeon crawl that requires you to coordinate one group led by Garek and a second led by the elven priest Ilastar Songbreeze – 500 bonus points if you recognize that deep cut, because I definitely had to look up who the heck he was and I practically eat, sleep, and breathe Warcraft. They remain separated for the first half of the mission, which created some interesting opportunities to use one group to complete an objective that helped the other progress. They then unite at the end for the final, dramatic push.

In an extremely heavily-telegraphed twist, Garek doesn't fare well in his confrontation with Rivendare, and ends up raised as one of the free-willed Forsaken in the main campaign. Taking his orders directly from Sylvanas and accompanied by her lieutenant, the Dark Ranger Anya, this free-roaming, quest-driven adventure revolves around establishing the Forsaken in the Undercity beneath the capital ruins. We also know Garek is destined to become the first Forsaken Paladin – an unorthodox combo that is soon to be playable in World of Warcraft – but I'm not sure how this transpires just yet.

Forsaken Kingdom also comes with a third, entirely new graphical style for Warcraft 3 called the "Definitive Edition" option. The idea was to address the complaints people had about 2020's divisive Reforged update, making Warcraft 3 look a bit more detailed and modern while preserving the feel of the original. At first, I wasn't super impressed with this direction. It doesn't look great zoomed in during cutscenes, to be honest. A lot of the textures are extremely flat, matte, and almost unfinished-looking. You can see visible pixels on some of the armor where it transitions from the faction blue to the metallic edging. And the lighting still comes off as pretty dated.

But when I loaded into a custom skirmish match against AI, I suddenly saw what they were going for. Playing zoomed out at a fast pace, I almost forgot I wasn't using the original 2003 graphics. It's like a magic trick. All the units and buildings look like how I remember them, just with higher fidelity. I suspect this will become the preferred way to play multiplayer and custom games for all but the most die-hard, low-polygon grognards.

It's a bit unfortunate to me, then, that these visual goodies are so unevenly distributed. The Forsaken Kingdom campaign can only be played with the Definitive Edition graphics. And, you know, that seems fair enough. Multiplayer and skirmish let you pick between Classic, Reforged, or Definitive Edition. But if you want to revisit the still frankly superb Reign of Chaos and Frozen Throne campaigns – and you really should! – they only support Classic or Reforged, not Definitive.

The other significant addition, and the one with a big impact on multiplayer, is Warcraft 3's first new tavern hero since the Alchemist and Firelord were added in 2004. This is the Forsaken Paladin, based on Garek of course. He's in a bit of a strange thematic spot. After all, there's already the Human Paladin hero, and the Death Knight was originally designed as sort of a negative mirror image of that. So where does that leave the Forsaken Paladin? Well, he is an undead neutral hero who can only heal the living, so he might be the least useful to Undead players, ironically. His Q ability is a dash that does more damage the more enemies it passes through, so he's quite mobile. As a strength hero, he is deadly in melee. His W is familiar to anyone who has played a WoW paladin with Consecration, which damages undead enemies and heals friendly living units in a small circle at his feet. He also has a passive aura that reduces magic damage taken and increases healing received. And his ult is an AoE purge/stun that heals nearby friendly units, with bonus healing and a short damage buff if the purge removed a debuff from them. This could definitely have some strong counterplay against certain builds, and I'm interested to see what pro players think of him.

I should also mention that the number of units in a control group has been doubled across all game modes. It's an ambitious change for a legacy game like this, and one I'm sure the old guard will groan about. But I think it's a positive one overall, from my spot down here in the tryhard seats.

Keep an eye out in the coming weeks for my final review of Forsaken Kingdom once I've gotten a chance to conquer the full campaign.

articles.title: StarCraft Devs Promise New Game Will Definitely Release in 2030
articles.summary: We got the chance to speak with the developers of the new StaCcraft game, who explained why they shared such a distant release date and even teased some potential gameplay elements.
articles.body:
We got the chance to speak with the developers of the new StarCraft game, who explained why they shared such a distant release date and even teased some potential gameplay elements for this highly-anticipated title.

StarCraft is finally getting a new game, and it’s taking a drastically different approach from its predecessors; instead of an RTS, Blizzard’s grisly sci-fi property is making its debut in the realm of open-world shooters, and it’s set to launch in 2030.

That’s a long way out from now, and it’s anyone’s guess as to what the world will look like in four years. We got the chance to ask the developers everyone’s burning question at Blizzcon 2026: Why announce the game if there’s still so much time left before it releases?

Dan Hay, GM & VP of StarCraft and AnaLee Haertling, Associate Director, told us that sharing a firm release date helps keep them “honest” — and yes, 2030 is a firm release date.

“You walk a funny line, because it’s like, you wanna tease, and we wanna say, ‘Hey, this is where we wanna land,’” Hay explained. “The reason why I love a really good date, is because the reality is that it puts a target. It allows us to say to a team that that’s what we’re going for. It’s a rallying cry, and we’re focused on that. We wanna make sure we deliver something that is fun, something that is powerful, and something that allows you to explore. But I also like the idea that there’s a frame that keeps us honest. And it says, ‘2030, let’s go.’”

When asked if 2030 was a solid date, Hay confirmed that it is, indeed, “solid.”

While Hay couldn’t tell us how long the game has been in development, he did share some insight into how hard the team is working to transform StarCraft into a world that feels like a living, breathing universe that’s both welcoming to new players and recognizable to longtime fans.

“I can’t tell you how long it’s been in development with the team, but I can tell you how long it’s been in development in my head, and it’s probably about 25 years,” he joked. “For us, I think what’s important is that we've gone out to find people who really love the brand. We’ve gone out to people who know the brand, who come back and really feel the love of the legacy. We’ve taken great pains and great care to make something that feels authentic, that when you walk through this world, you recognize it.

“It's a tricky thing. It’s a bit of a knife’s edge. You wanna build something that is welcoming and inviting to new players but you wanna make sure it feels real. That when you walk into a bar it feels like a bar from the original world. When you meet players and characters and you see them, they've got the weapons and the armor and it feels authentic and it feels real.”

Hay went on to drop a few subtle hints at what players can expect in this new game, saying that StarCraft will bring into sharp focus the rough edges of its world, along with the visceral feeling of being a soldier fighting against massive, deadly creatures.

“We wanna show that it’s rough tools out there, it's a difficult world, it's filled with warfare and different factions and different groups of people, and they don’t always get along, and we wanted to bring that to bear from the very beginning,” he told us.

“When you think about what StarCraft will allow you to do, and we thought about how we tell this story — this is the way to tell that story. To be boots on the ground, to be down in the muck and the dirt, and to feel the tension of it.

“There was something really powerful — and I have to be careful not to give too much away here — I remember seeing the first time that a Hydralisk was 10 feet tall, and it was basically snapping at me. And I’ve got a gun and I’ve got armor, and I’m feeling like I’m down in the dirt and I’m feeling the weight of it. Emily was just talking about the deployment of the barracks. What’s super powerful about it is the moment you drop down on the ground, your perspective changes. It doesn’t feel like you’re a god looking down at this and you’re detached. It feels like, ‘My God, I'm in the middle of this. Every decision matters. Everything I do feels like it has gravitas.’”

He also dove into why Blizzard chose to take StarCraft in such a wildly different direction, rather than staying with the series’ RTS roots — and in doing so, shed some light on a few possible key gameplay elements, one of which is using an enemy as a “tool” against another enemy.

“For us, when we think about the themes and we think about the opportunity for you to be on the battlefield and for you to go out and think about the vista, the opportunity to explore, and then to discover, and then to disrupt. It’s incredibly unique. And then when you think about the different factions that there are, we just wanted people to go out into these worlds and actually get a sense of what it’s like to meet these different groups.

“Again, I really wanna talk about this stuff, but I also have to hold some stuff back, but what's really important is you think about some of these different factions in StarCraft, and you think about what they bring and you think about the way that it feels. I have imagery in my head right now that I can be careful not to describe, but I’m seeing an awful lot of biomass, and I’m seeing a lot of stuff we were hinting at. If you look at the teaser and you start to see that moment where the barracks is flying in and you look at the planet, you’ll actually see all the things that are alive on that planet and get a sense of that feel.

“For us, it felt right to put you down on the ground in the middle of people that are fighting and they don’t agree. This feeling of, ‘The enemy of my enemy is a tool to be used.’ We felt like the open world and the opportunity to explore and to discover and of course to disrupt and to use my enemy against another enemy felt really powerful.”

StarCraft is still a ways out, but you can catch up on all the other exciting news Blizzard had to offer in our round-up blog for the event's Opening Ceremony and take a peek at everything that's available to play right now.

Virginia (she/her) is IGN’s News Editor. With ten years of experience reporting on games and entertainment, she’s got a storied background in the fighting game community, influencer news, and viral online trends. Find her on Twitter at @TheeMissGlaze .

articles.title: From the Team That *Almost* Made Blade, Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother Takes Mahershala Ali on an Action Odyssey
articles.summary: Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother review: Mahershala Ali joins his would-be Blade director as a devout sword-wielding assassin.
articles.body:
Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother arrives in theaters on September 25. This review is based on a screening from the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival.

Once upon a time, Oscar-winning actor Mahershala Ali was meant to play slick vampire hunter Blade for Marvel Studios under Mogul Mowgli and Bait director Bassam Tariq. The project never materialized, but it led the Muslim actor-filmmaker pair to team up for Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother, a surprisingly thoughtful, action-tinged crime drama about a devout hit man trying to find breast milk for his infant daughter. This takes him through mosques and strip clubs alike in rural Virginia, laying out a visually and emotionally multifaceted journey across a heightened American landscape.

The result — born of Tariq’s own experience trying to feed his newborn son while his wife was in the ICU — beats with a lived emotional authenticity, while unfolding against a borderline satirical modern United States whose religious and cultural concerns inform the movie’s sprawling drama. Ali plays sword-wielding contract killer (and former Quran teacher) Latif, a man whose strict and sometimes paradoxical principles — like using blades but never guns, although the result is just as vicious — are challenged when his wife Khadija (Shakirah DeMesier) suddenly dies. This leaves him to care for his rebellious teenage daughter Fatiha (Adia), his delightfully brash adolescent son Qadir (Jahleel Kamara), and his hungry baby girl (who doesn’t take well to formula) by any means necessary.

The repetition of the film’s title is explained numerous times in voiceover as an Islamic hadith (a prophetic edict) about the central role of mothers in Muslim tradition; in a list of important figures in one’s life, they would occupy the top three spots. Before we ever meet the radiant Khadija in brief flashbacks, Latif is informed of her death by phone call during a darkly comedic scene where he’s just finished butchering a target before clumsily disposing of the corpse. Her absence looms large over the movie, forcing Latif to fill her enormous shoes in ways he may not be prepared for, as little hints of his personal code are doled out through dialogue. He kills Christian white supremacists and Islamic terrorists alike — anyone who poses a danger to innocent people or his community at large — though his vigilantism is largely backgrounded and, for better or worse, left to the imagination.

Awkward exchanges stemming from his conservative approach to women complicate his mission to feed his daughter, but his former associate Mike (Laith Nakli), an Arab American security specialist, is eager to help… for a price. Mike’s unruly nephew (a scummy Abubakr Ali) and former student of Latif’s has not only been rejected by their community for his salacious content creation, but has a target on his back owing to suspicions of pornography and human trafficking courtesy of Korean American pastor (and respected former soldier) Hwan Yoon, played by John Cho in a maniacally fun role. Should Latif take out the heavily guarded Hwan, his needs will be taken care of, but the pious assassin wants out of the game.

Tariq crafts a detailed simulacrum of modern America split by the pull of religion — Latif’s Islam, Hwan’s Evangelicalism, and the Mormonism of a kindly neighbor — but bound by the search for community, no matter how warped. As much as Hwan is satirized as a gun-toting extremist playing to a Confederate flag-waving fan base, the purity of his convictions makes him both sympathetic and utterly terrifying. This in turn makes for a powerful mirror for Latif, whose own hard-fought beliefs are forced to waver in the face of unusually difficult circumstances, playing out at great length through arguments and verbal dilemmas. The action is surprisingly scant, but its brief eruptions are intense, realistic, and soaked in both blood and remorse.

The majority of the drama revolves around the loss of Latif’s wife and the hole it leaves in his heart, affording Ali the chance to deliver a devastating performance which Tariq and cinematographer Katelin Arizmendi accentuate through sweltering contrast and saturation. The light bouncing off Latif’s sweat-drenched brow adds as much to the movie’s bleakly comedic mood as Son Lux’s bouncy, intense score. As darkly funny as the film may be — thanks in large part to Fatiha’s rejection of her father and his faith — its drama is treated both seriously and tenderly. This is especially true in the moments Latif has to confront either Khadija’s family, like her Christianized brother (played by Tramell Tillman), or domineering members of his community, like his imam (Giancarlo Esposito), all of whom seem at least vaguely aware of his line of work.

Where the movie falters most is in its refusal to detail what Latif’s code actually looks and feels like, owing to a lack of preceding moments where we get to observe his job (or rather, his mission) unfolding as usual. This might have gone a long way toward dramatizing what it actually means for him to break his solemn vows; without this contrast, a number of turning points and major decisions feel robbed of their potential weight. However, the film is no less aesthetically inviting, accentuating fearful close-ups with spiritual halos as its conflicted antihero struggles with his duties as a father and man of faith in a violent world that has shaped him violently in return.

articles.summary: El nuevo jugador de Philadelphia bajaba tres puntos de media respecto al año pasado
articles.body: Durante toda la historia del NBA 2K parece que hay cosas que no cambian como el tiro de tres, los mates, los tapones...o la presencia de LeBron James entre los jugadores más valorados del videojuego. Y es que 'el rey' ha estado dominando tanto en la liga como en el juego durante dos décadas, algo que, como es lógico se está acabando por la edad de LeBron, el que, pese a tener 41 años sigue estando entre la élite de ambos mundos. Pero es cierto que los mejores días del alero ya han pasado, primero en la vida real, donde ya el año pasado bajó su promedio de puntos a 20,9, convirtiéndose por primera vez en su vida en una 'segunda espada' tras la llegada de Luka Doncic a Lakers. Pero además en NBA 2K 27 hemos visto como también ha bajado, en este caso del 94 de valoración del año pasado al 91 de este. Así, el nuevo jugador de los Philadelphia 76ers contará en el NBA 2K27 con la tercera peor valoración de su carrera, superando solamente su primer y segundo año en la liga, es decir, el 78 del NBA 2K4 y el 88 del NBA 2K5, o dicho de otra manera, LeBron James está en su peor momento en el videojuego de los últimos 22 años. Pese a esta bajada 'el rey' sigue estando en la élite del videojuego, ya que, aunque ya no pueda competir los primeros puestos a Shai, Jokic o Wembanyama, sigue estando entre los 20 mejores jugadores del NBA 2K27, igualando en media a jugadores como Jaylen Brown, Joel Embiid y Booker y superando a superestrellas de la liga como Haliburton, Anthony Davis, Jamal Murray o Austin Reaves entre otros muchos. Además este año Lebron tiene muchas opciones de mejorar su valoración a lo largo de la temporada, pues el proyecto de Philadelphia debería ganar muchos partidos y las medias van subiendo y bajando en función del desempeño del jugador. Así que, si es importante en un equipo muy ganador, seguro que vemos al 'rey' subir su estatus dentro de la liga y del videojuego.

articles.title: Scooby-Doo: Origins Reveals Cute New Photo of the Live-Action Dog
articles.body:
Netflix announced Sunday that production has officially wrapped in Atlanta on their upcoming series Scooby-Doo: Origins . The streaming service also released a new photo of the titular good boy, which can be seen in the image gallery below.

Scooby-Doo: Origins marks the first time a real Great Dane has portrayed the beloved canine member of the Mystery Inc. gang.

“During their final summer at camp, old friends Shaggy and Daphne get embroiled in a haunting mystery surrounding a lonely lost Great Dane puppy that may have been a witness to a supernatural murder,” according to the official synopsis.

“Together with the pragmatic and scientific townie, Velma, and the strange, but ever so handsome new kid, Freddy, they set out to solve the case that is pulling each of them into a creepy nightmare that threatens to expose all of their secrets.”

Other cast members include Paul Walter Hauser, Rusty Schwimmer, Peter Macon, Jona Xiao, Dani Deetté, Elysée Sanvillé, Alex Isles, Avery Kristen Pohl, Pamela Mitchell, Ross Kimball, Sara Gilbert, Wynn Everett, Sauriyan Sapkota, Bruce McGill, André Benjamin, and Cathy Moriarity.

Josh Appelbaum and Scott Rosenberg serve as executive producers and showrunners.

Executive producers include Greg Berlanti , Sarah Schechter, Leigh London Redman (via Berlanti Productions and its overall deal with Warner Bros. Television), André Nemec, Jeff Pinkner, and Adrienne Erickson (via Midnight Radio), and Toby Haynes (EP/Episode 101 Director).

Scooby-Doo: Origins will launch globally in 2027.

articles.title: World of Warcraft: Forever Devs Explain Why the Game Makes WoW 2 Unlikely
articles.summary: World of Warcraft: Forever developers Kris Zierhut and Mike Nuthals detail the game's new features and explain why a WoW 2 sequel is unnecessary.
articles.body:
World of Warcraft: Forever, a Classic+ iteration of the long-running franchise that lets players return to an updated vanilla Azeroth featuring new zones, dungeons, raids, and more, was announced at yesterday’s BlizzCon 2026 Opening Ceremony. And now, the game’s developers are revealing why they think the new take on the classic game (along with the numerous other WoW updates announced yesterday) renders the long-speculated World of Warcraft 2 unnecessary.

“I think one of the things that's singularly great about WoW is we have this game and this world and this design that has been continuously developed for the last 25 years,” Zierhut says. “And we keep making it better. We made the graphics better, we made the rendering better, we made the lighting better; all that new stuff we showed on stage today.

“But we've also made the way the engine draws things move more efficiently. The way the server runs, handling players and moving them around, and all the things that handle spells and combat, all of that's been made more efficient and better over the years. We have this incredible engine and server infrastructure driving the game that is second to none. Why would you throw that away and start over?”

Zierhut went on to say that, in addition to the technical advancements in World of Warcraft: Forever, the team is still invested in building the story of the current WoW universe.

“It’s not like there's something wrong with the story,” Zierhut says. “We love the story. So going back to the beginning [with World of Warcraft: Forever], there's a chance to explore that story in new and different ways. So it's really hard to say, ‘Well, what would a WoW 2 give you that World of Warcraft: Forever isn't already giving you?’”

As revealed on stage yesterday, World of Warcraft: Forever won’t merely be a rehashed update of the original. In addition to “updated world visuals and lighting,” the game will feature 10 and 20-player raids, more than 1,000 new quests, new race and class combos, a new Skyborne race, and more. Nuthals and Zierhut say there are a few key features they’re most eager for fans to experience.

“I'm so excited for our players to uncover all of our new items,” Nuthals says. “All of the dungeons and raids have had an itemization pass. There's so much new to explore. I'm really anxious for our players to get in there and explore the world, find all the cool little nooks and crannies, find their really cool loot and just have a great time.

[And] the thing I think I'm most excited about with our raids are the raid sizes. We're going to have Barrow Deeps which will be our 10-player raid. We're going to have the Hyjal Summit, which will be 20, and then Onyxia will be 40. I think the thing that gets me most excited about that is getting folks to find social groups and friends to fill those groups up.”

World of Warcraft: Forever's New Camping Feature Explained

“The thing I'm most excited about is the camping feature,” Zierhut says. “So you may remember in World of Warcraft in the past, you could put down a cooking fire and you could sit and cook your food. The cooking fire has now become the basic campfire. And while you're sitting there waiting, because you have to sit there for a minute, another player [could walk] by and they add to it. And now you are [all] there and you’ve got to wait a minute you're like, ‘Hey, what quest are you working on? Oh, we’re working on the same quest. Hey, how about we group up?’ And that's the moment the friendships, relationships, and guilds are born. And I'm really excited about what that's going to do for our game.”

While World of Warcraft: Forever will include many new updates for players to explore, Zierhut and Nuthals say it won’t stray too far from what players love about the original.

“We're not going to make massive changes to the lore,” Zierhut says. “We're not going to change the way the world feels, but we can maybe have a slightly different sequence of what's happening. It doesn't contradict what was in Classic, but it's a little bit different. So we have room for a slightly different story. Nobody has to worry about problems with the timeline.”

“Our pillars are very universal, core to the experience of playing Classic WoW,” Nuthals says. “That’s always what we're thinking of in the back of our head. It's exhilarating to see what our players are going to do when they get into it and play it.”

World of Warcraft: Forever launches November 4.

articles.title: ‘Hell Yes!’ - Diablo 4 Dev Team Reacts to the Franchise’s New Netflix Show
articles.summary: Diablo 4’s lead developers discuss their excitement for the new Diablo Netflix animated series, the game's Switch 2 port, and Season of Hell's Legacy.
articles.body:
Among the many announcements during yesterday’s BlizzCon Opening Ceremony, the news that Diablo is getting its own show at Netflix has at least one of the franchise’s development teams chomping at the bit. Yesterday, Blizzard president Johanna Faries revealed that a Diablo animated series is in the works but admitted she “can’t spill the beans” just yet on exactly what the new show entails.

Regardless, the development team behind Diablo 4 says it’s quite possibly the reveal they are most excited about, even more so than the news that Diablo 5 is coming out in 2029 , Diablo 4 is getting a Switch 2 port, Spawn is coming to Diablo Immortal, and the arrival of the Amazon class. I sat down with Brent Gibson, Diablo 4’s Game Director, and Owen Leach, Season Lead for Diablo 4 - Hell’s Legacy, after yesterday’s news to break everything down.

“Even though I have no information and can't share anything, the fact that we're getting a show [is what I’m most excited about]," Gibson says. “I'm a story guy. I want to see more story, as much story as you can get. We’re narrowing in on finding the creative team [for the show] and we're delivering on what Johanna was saying, [that] we're Blizzard Entertainment. I think Diablo's a perfect world to start telling those stories, so I couldn't be more happy that we're getting a show.”

During yesterday’s presentation, Faries also noted that Overwatch, Warcraft and “perhaps even some…other [Blizzard] universes” could get their own series. But for now, news of a Diablo adaptation is proving to be more than enough to keep the development teams buzzing.

“The show is my fan answer [for what I’m most excited about],” Leach says. “I've seen animated shows on Netflix and I'm like, ‘Hell yes.’"

“I think this world of IPs existing and multiple media is the Wild West,” Gibson adds. “You actually can't predict how those mechanisms work. You watch other games that have gotten their shows and how that's plussed things up and changed things. Fallout is a really great example of that. You see this massive resurgence in the game because of the show and I love that. I have no idea where it's going but it's the right time and I'm super excited about it.”

Along with the new Netflix show, Gibson and Leach say there’s plenty for fans to be excited about in the Diablo universe.

“Being the Season Lead of Hell's Legacy, I am so excited for Diablo to be in Diablo 4,” Leach says. “I'm losing my mind and that's just one boss. We’ve got 20 new bosses. Na-Krul from Diablo: Hellfire. I'm sure people in the crowd are going to lose their minds when they find out about that. So September 15th, I can't wait. I'm really excited for players to celebrate the 30th anniversary with us.”

Gibson says that he’s also looking forward to players getting their hands on Diablo 4: Age of Hatred Collection when it launches on Nintendo Switch 2 on September 15.

“It's about damn time,” Gibson says. “We've been talking about what it means to be on handheld platforms since day one. I'm floored at the level of quality they were able to get it to. There is an audience there that we haven't been servicing. I think it was on a list of top 10 games that everybody wanted to have on the Switch 2 from launch. And I'm like, ‘Yeah, me too. Here we go.’ So I'm very happy.”

“I like the flexibility of being able to play wherever I want,” Leach adds. “I used to play on the Steam Deck, but having a specific build for the console is even better. So now I'm playing on my couch because I'm lazy and then some days I'm playing on my PC. That's how we do it.”

For more on BlizzCon 2026, check out everything announced at the Opening Ceremony .

articles.title: The Witcher 3 Geralt Skin for Diablo 4 Barbarians Revealed — but There's a Catch
articles.summary: CD Projekt and Blizzard have released a first look at the Geralt-themed Barbarian skin for Diablo 4, but you'll need to preorder The Witcher 3 expansion Songs of the Past on Battle.net to get it.
articles.body:
CD Projekt and Blizzard have released a first look at the Geralt-themed Barbarian skin for Diablo 4 , but you'll need to preorder The Witcher 3 expansion Songs of the Past on Battle.net to get it.

During BlizzCon 2026, CD Projekt’s Expert Community and Social Media Manager Amelia Korzycka and Level Design Lead Miles Tost appeared as guests on the 30 Years of Battle.net panel to reveal the skin, which will be available to Battle.net players who pre-purchase Songs of the Past (it’s only available to wishlist right now), or buy the expansion when it launches. That means the Geralt skin is locked behind Battle.net, which in turn means Steam players, for example, miss out.

This, as you can imagine, isn’t going down particularly well with Diablo 4 players who already own The Witcher 3 on non-Battle.net platforms. Remastered is coming to Steam as a free upgrade on September 29, 2026 for anyone who already owns the base game. So, those who already own The Witcher 3 on Steam (at this point, who doesn't?) and are interested in Songs of the Past are probably going to buy it on Valve's platform, and probably don't want to rebuy The Witcher 3 on Battle.net just so they can get the Geralt skin for Diablo 4.

“Not paying for a second copy of a 15-year-old game that most people who would play it probably already own,” one person said on social media. “Thx though Blizzard.”

“He looks so bad,” another said in response to Geralt’s face in the image shown during the panel itself. “I'm glad tho because I had zero desire to preorder a game in the worst launcher ever just to get this. I really hope they sold it separately in the future.”

The Geralt skin is also coming under fire from some Diablo 4 fans who were angered by Blizzard's confirmation yesterday that the game will not get any further expansions. Diablo game director Brent Gibson told PC Gamer : "We're all focused on [Diablo 4] seasons and getting to Diablo 5. We feel like we told the Story of Hatred. We had a great conclusion with Lord of Hatred with what we have with Mephisto, and we are moving towards telling the Story of Terror." Diablo 4 launched June 2023. Diablo 5 is due out at some point in 2029.

“For us creatively, stuff like this is super fun because it puts us as creatives in a position where we have to think, how do we make these worlds collide in a way that gives respect and pays respect to both of the source materials, Diablo and The Witcher in this context?” Tost said of the Geralt skin during the Battle.net BlizzCon panel.

“So when we look at these kind of things we first try to find the overlap. What makes sense? Diablo of course, talking about classes, looking at the roster, we relatively quickly landed at the Barbarian as the place where we could imagine adding Geralt-inspired content. They’re both masters of physical prowess. They have trained all their lives to become super strong and powerful melee combatants. The Barbarian is capable of wielding multiple weapons at the same time. Geralt doesn’t wield them at the same time, but he does use two swords: the iconic steel for humans and silver for monsters.

“And you can see here — for those of you in the know — that this armor is heavily inspired by Geralt’s iconic Kaer Morhen armor. There’s a bit of Barbarian sprinkled on top… you see all the fur. I think you can see here how we’re trying to create collaborations like these in a way that makes sense for both teams and worlds and also fans. I hope you can see here how we have created something that feels right at home in Sanctuary.”

CD Projekt said that next year even more Witcher-themed content will hit Diablo 4, with more details to be revealed at a later date. “This skin, taking Geralt’s style into the hellscapes of Sanctuary, is the first piece of Witcher-inspired content coming to Diablo 4, and more is in the works, coming to Blizzard’s action-RPG in 2027,” CD Projekt added.

Every CD Projekt Red Game In Development

Meanwhile, CD Projekt announced that Cyberpunk 2077 , its expansion Phantom Liberty, and the Ultimate Edition are coming to Battle.net later this year as its partnership with Blizzard expands. Meanwhile, Blizzard’s Overwatch will get Cyberpunk: Edgerunners and Edgerunners 2-themed content in 2027. Sequel animated series Cyberpunk: Edgerunners 2 premieres on Netflix on October 20.

articles.title: Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom Completes Aardman’s Farm Feature Trilogy With a Halloween Treat For All Ages
articles.summary: Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom review: The residents of Mossy Bottom farm are baaaaack for their first Halloween adventure.
articles.body:
Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom is in theaters on September 18.

In this 50th year celebrating Aardman Animations, most think of the ongoing adventures of Wallace & Gromit. But the more humble MVP of the stop-motion studio continues to be Shaun the Sheep, first introduced in the 1995 Academy Award-winning short, A Close Shave. He and his Mossy Bottom Farms flock have since starred in multiple series, shorts, and a trilogy of feature films. The third installment of that trilogy, Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom, is a love letter to the Universal Monsters era of filmmaking that’s a delightful homage to silent era visual comedy.

In keeping with 2015’s Shaun the Sheep Movie and 2019’s A Shaun the Sheep Movie: Farmageddon, The Beast of Mossy Bottom continues to keep its world and characters basic and easy to follow. This Halloween-centric story opens at Mossy Bottom farm, which is run by the clueless Farmer and his more competent sheepdog with an exaggerated overbite, Bitzer (both vocalized by comedian John Sparkes). Left to play in the fields is his flock, led by the super-creative and adventurous Shaun (Justin Fletcher). Aware that the Farmer is in general a liability, the flock has grown a secret pumpkin patch that they’ve carefully nurtured and grown to perfection for their Halloween Hoedown, nestled away from the Farmer’s eyes and extremely clumsy feet.

The Farmer, of course, still finds a way to ruin the patch, which spurs a despondent Shaun to come up with a fix so little Timmy and their flock can have their party. Finding a handmade science book in the barn, Shaun devolves into a mini-Frankenstein — including experimenting in his windmill lab — to create a serum he’ll put on their pumpkin seeds so they’ll grow back in time for Halloween. And boy do they, uncontrollably so, which puts Shaun on the back hoof fixing his fix.

In the film’s intertwined “B” plot, the Farmer has a secret crush on the local Vet (Nina Sosanya), but he’s feeling embarrassed by the retreating creep of his hairline. He also seeks a quick remedy when he stumbles upon a bottle of old hair growth (newly filled with the excess of Shaun’s serum), and decides to use it to get confident enough to ask the lady doc out. You can imagine the hairy mess that ensues.

The strength of Mark Burton and Giles Pilbrow’s screenplay, and most Shaun and Aardman features for that matter, is that each film’s increasingly dire situations don't come from overcomplicated plots; rather, they derive from the escalation of the characters’ actions and the domino effect, which makes for simple narratives. Here, that translates into a movie younger viewers can easily follow while still appealing to older viewers with its classic movie underpinnings for the Halloween season. Plus, the writers and animators have ambitiously filled every frame with horror cinema visual easter eggs, endless sight gags, and great character performances. The Beast of Mossy Bottom is almost dialogue-free, but it all works because first-time feature directors Steve Cox and Matthew Walker have kept the core narrative clear and loaded the film with generational gags that cleverly reference today’s horrors as well as bits from James Whale’s Frankenstein and Steven Spielberg’s Jaws.

It’s also appreciated that the directors have expanded the farm to extend into the unsettling woods of Mossingham, added that set piece-worthy windmill, folded in the expanded Mossingham citizenry, and included a whole sea-set action sequence. That level of scale for The Beast of Mossy Bottom keeps the pokey farm from feeling too small for a cinematic story, and continues to push the limits of the stop-motion wizardry of the Aardman Animations team. Speaking of which, the animators have outdone themselves by including massive amounts of moving hair to their animation repertoire as the Farmer goes full Sasquatch; they also weave in spritzing water and aquatic critters. It’s easy to forget, and take for granted, that every single character and locale is handmade and individually manipulated by animators, making this another stunning achievement and demonstration of the studio’s patience and craftsmanship.

Special kudos also go to Natalie Holt’s score, which does a tremendous amount of emotional heavy lifting in what is essentially a silent film. She and her orchestra land jokes with their flourishes à la Carl Stalling’s Looney Tunes and Merrie Melodies compositions, or wholesale create emotional moments that they mine with notes in between the character grunts or gibberish talk.

Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom is a great addition to the Aardman farm trilogy and to their larger production history. It’s clearly made by a team of silent-era horror cinema nerds and some of the quickest punsters in the business. It’s heartening to see the studio’s continuing commitment to the stop-motion technique while honoring what’s come before in the horror genre. Though it may not be as slick or elevated as Wallace & Gromit: Vengeance Most Fowl, The Beast of Mossy Bottom deserves a theatrical watch and to become a future Halloween classic.

articles.title: Diablo 5 Director Confirms Game is Already in Full Production
articles.summary: Diablo 5 is officially in full production and coming in 2029. Game Director Joe Shely reveals the sequel will feature more classes, procedural worlds, and jump 100 years into the future.
articles.body:
While tons of new updates are coming to Diablo, including a new Netflix series , Diablo 4 Season 15, a Switch 2 port , and more, the biggest reveal for the franchise at BlizzCon 2026 was the announcement of Diablo V , coming in 2029.

IGN sat down exclusively with the team behind the upcoming game, including Game Director Joe Shely, Narrative Director Jennifer Helper, and Production Director Tiffany Wat, who gave us tons of new details about Diablo 5, including how it’s already past early development.

IGN: I know probably nobody has missed the Diablo 5 announcement, but can you guys just kind of give sort of a top-level view of what the game will be?

Joe Shely: Diablo 5 is a world where Sanctuary has fallen and Diablo has won. That means that the world is in an apocalypse. The fate that players have been trying to prevent for many years throughout other Diablo games has happened. Other heroes rose up, tried to stop Diablo, and failed. Diablo sits on the throne of Westmarch and has conquered all of the Western continent.

The Reason Diablo 5 is Set 100 Years After Diablo 4

IGN: Diablo 4 still has some life in it. What are you planning to achieve in Diablo 5 that you don't think that as a whole would've been able to be achievable in Diablo 4?

Shely: Diablo 4 has bright support. It's fully supported by the team. We were just announcing earlier today, coming to Diablo 4, the Amazon, the Season of Hell's legacy, Diablo 4 is coming to Switch 2, and there will continue to be ongoing support for Diablo 4. There's many reasons for players to keep playing. And of course, we've been in development for some time on Diablo 5. We're in full production and it's been really an exciting time for us to be able to get to share it with players.

Jennifer Helper: We’re bringing Diablo back and Diablo should never be an “and another thing” in a Diablo game. We need a full campaign and full story based around Diablo. [With Diablo 5], we've jumped a hundred years ahead to tell that story so that Diablo 4 has lots of space to continue their story and their development while we're doing Diablo 5.

Diablo 5 Will Have “More Classes Than You’ve Ever Seen”

Tiffany Wat: [Diablo 5] is an opportunity for us to really lean into some of the incredible innovations, both on the technology, but also on the gameplay and system side. We are bringing more classes than you’ve ever seen in a Diablo game. We talked about bringing back the procedural world, something that was really popular in prior Diablo games, and we leaned into it in Diablo 4 with our dungeon system. In Diablo 5, we really felt that this is such a really fun and integral way to be playing Diablo, and we wanted to bring it back to both the overworld and the dungeon systems.

Joe talks to his team a lot about the importance of constant discovery and not knowing what's around the corner. That adds an element of danger to the world of Sanctuary and that really ties well with the story that Jennifer and her team are trying to tell. Being able to tie all of that together and really reach for the gameplay ambitions that Joe and his team have, it made a lot of sense for us to just embark on a sequel, and we've been doing it for a little bit of time now.

Diablo 5 Will Be Less Open World Because Diablo Has Destroyed Everything

IGN: It seems like you guys are going for more of that traditional overworld that people travel to in different spaces. So we're not going to have that open world vibe like we did in Diablo 4.

Wat: There are no more towns because Diablo and his Dread Commanders have completely destroyed Sanctuary. And so that caravan that you are gathering, these members that you have met, survivors of Sanctuary that are coming along with you to try and just survive, figure out what's going on with Diablo, you're moving from region to region and that gives us a chance to really show what Sanctuary looks like when it's under the Lord of Terror and see the different ways that the Dread Commanders have twisted the world. Joe and I worked together on monsters for over a decade now on Diablo, and man, the monsters team is cooking. So being able to see the twisted, disgusting, horrifying demons that show up at different times in different worlds that you're loading into is just really, really cool.

IGN: When Diablo 5 launches, support seems like it'll continue for Diablo 4 and other games. Do you foresee any challenges with not just player retention, but overall content creation when you have basically five Diablo games in rotation for people to come back to season after season?

Wat: We have dedicated teams for each of those games because those games are important to us and they're really important for our community. I think it really gives us a really great opportunity to be able to collaborate together, to talk with one another. Even though we might be distinct teams, we still work together quite closely because ultimately we are making games for the Diablo community. I think it's the best time to be a Diablo fan.

IGN: The ARPG market is getting larger. How does Diablo evolve in a market when the target audience is split across multiple titles? Do you look to these games to see what types of new things they're making to inject into your games?

Shely: Of course. ARPGs are ultimately systems games underneath everything. And we play everything that relates to Diablo or could give us an idea of what players are enjoying. But in particular, the way that we approach it is by focusing on the things that are really core to Diablo and Diablo really excels at. Things like evolving our combat model, things like making a game that's approachable and has an incredible campaign. We want this to be our best campaign ever.

Some of the crunchiness of Diablo 2 that really speaks to many of the core ARPG players has inspired Diablo 5 with things like stat requirements returning on items, item tiers, which is very much inspired by Diablo 2, and even things like the return of the belt slot or multi-slot items in your inventory.

IGN: Can you talk a little bit actually about the return of the belt slot and about the itemization in Diablo 5 versus say Diablo 4 and how you guys plan to approach that?

Shely : I mean, the simple answer is that the belt slot is generally a more exciting slot than the pants slot. The belt slot is just a reflection of the way that we look at the suite of items that the player can equip. And we always want to balance that so that you have the right amount of different pieces of your gear that you're chasing both between the weapons and the armor. So in terms of evolving the visual style, one of the things that the belt slot lets us do is make gear sets that are more cohesive between the chest armor and the pants.

IGN: We see that Diablo is coming back now in Diablo 4, starting with season 15. You've got however many more seasons between now and Diablo 5 launches. Is there anything you're worried about with Diablo’s implementation maybe in Diablo 4 versus how he's going to appear in Diablo 5?

Helper: We also not only are a hundred years ahead, we are back on the Western continent. So Diablo 4’s content is all in the East and we are back in Westmarch, which everyone is familiar with from the first three games. And Westmarch has expanded over the entire Western continent. So we've got a lot of future history of the Western continent that we haven't seen in a really long time that we're going to be able to cover that is a completely open space for us.

IGN: Last question. When will we learn more about Diablo 5?

Shely: When we decided to announce that we've been working on Diablo V, we wanted to make sure that we shared some meaningful updates, talking about classes, talking about the return of the Demon Hunter, the Monk, new classes like the Plague Knight , things like itemization that we talked about before. And we want to continue that conversation. And in particular, the reason to talk about the game now and continue that conversation into 2027, when we'll share more about it, is to be able to talk with players, talk with everyone out there who loves Diablo, and build the game alongside them and by listening to the things that they want.
